records.source: τῇ ἐλευθερίᾳ ἡμᾶς Χριστὸς ἠλευθέρωσεν· στήκετε οὖν καὶ μὴ πάλιν ζυγῷ δουλείας ἐνέχεσθε.
records.gloss: For the freedom us Christ set free; stand firm therefore and not again in a yoke of slavery be held.
pieces: Freedom was {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}'s purpose when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} set us free. So stand firm, and do not let yourselves be held again under a yoke of slavery.

L.1: For freedom {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not again be held fast in a yoke of slavery.

R.1: {{christos:Christ|The Messiah}} set us free so that we would live as free people. So stand firm. Do not let anyone put a slave's yoke on you again.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "for freedom Christ set us free" as a sentence of its own
alternatives: "stand firm in the freedom with which Christ set us free", joining the clause to the command
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add a relative word and make the opening part of the command to stand firm, the reading behind the King James Version. The SBLGNT text, with the earliest manuscripts, has a complete statement followed by a raised dot, then the command. Either way Paul says that Christ has freed them and they must hold on to that freedom.

decisions.choice: "for freedom": freedom is the purpose of Christ's act
alternatives: "with freedom" or "by freedom": freedom as the means
decisions.reason: The dative τῇ ἐλευθερίᾳ stands first for emphasis beside the verb from the same root (ἐλευθερόω). Paul is saying what Christ freed them for: to live as free people, not to pass from one slavery into another. The word picks up the free woman and her children of 4:22-31.

decisions.choice: a yoke of slavery: the law taken up as a burden that binds
decisions.reason: A yoke is the wooden bar laid on the necks of working animals, and it was a common picture for being under another's rule. ἐνέχεσθε means to be held fast or caught in something. "Again" tells Gentile believers that taking the law as their master would be like returning to the slavery they knew under the elemental powers (4:3, 4:8-9).

decisions.choice: freedom stated first as the purpose
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say outright that freedom was the purpose, since the bare phrase is unclear in plain English.

decisions.choice: slavery (L, B); a slave's yoke (R)
decisions.reason: "Slavery" at every level, as the style guide keeps it where slavery under the law is set against freedom (m3).

records.heading: Stand firm in your freedom

records.source: Ἴδε ἐγὼ Παῦλος λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι ἐὰν περιτέμνησθε Χριστὸς ὑμᾶς οὐδὲν ὠφελήσει.
records.gloss: Look, I Paul say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ you nothing will profit.
pieces: Listen! I, Paul, am telling you: if you have yourselves circumcised, {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} will do you no good at all.

L.2: Look, I, Paul, say to you that if you get circumcised, {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} will profit you nothing.

R.2: Listen to me! I, Paul, am telling you this: if you go ahead and get circumcised, {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} will be of no use to you at all.

decisions.choice: circumcision taken up as a requirement for belonging to God's people
alternatives: circumcision as a mere physical rite with no further meaning
decisions.reason: The present tense of περιτέμνησθε speaks of Gentile believers who would now undergo circumcision because the agitators said they must (6:12-13). Paul himself had Timothy circumcised (Acts 16:3), so the rite as such is not the issue (5:6); taking it on as a condition of standing before God is, as verses 3-4 explain.

decisions.choice: Paul stakes his own authority on the warning
decisions.reason: Ἴδε calls for attention, and Paul names himself with the emphatic "I". He writes as the apostle who first brought them the gospel (1:1, 4:13).

decisions.choice: if you go ahead and get circumcised
decisions.reason: Readable brings out the present tense: a step the Galatians were thinking of taking.

records.source: μαρτύρομαι δὲ πάλιν παντὶ ἀνθρώπῳ περιτεμνομένῳ ὅτι ὀφειλέτης ἐστὶν ὅλον τὸν νόμον ποιῆσαι.
records.gloss: And I testify again to every man being circumcised that a debtor he is the whole the law to do.
pieces: I insist once more to every man who has himself circumcised: he puts himself under obligation to carry out the entire law.

L.3: And I testify again to every man who gets circumcised that he is a debtor to do the whole law.

R.3: I will say it again to every man who gets circumcised: he then has to obey every part of the law.

decisions.choice: under obligation, bound like a debtor to pay in full
alternatives: a debtor in a merely financial sense
decisions.reason: ὀφειλέτης is someone who owes a debt. Circumcision was the sign of the covenant given through Moses, so a man who takes it on as a requirement takes on the whole law with it. Paul has already said that the law curses everyone who does not keep all of it (3:10).

decisions.choice: "again" repeats the warning of verse 2
alternatives: "again" recalls an earlier warning given in person
decisions.reason: Paul restates verse 2 with a solemn word of testimony; he may also be recalling what he told them when he was with them. The point is the same.

decisions.choice: has himself circumcised / gets circumcised
decisions.reason: The Greek is a present participle in the middle or passive voice: a man who has the rite done to him.

records.source: κατηργήθητε ἀπὸ Χριστοῦ οἵτινες ἐν νόμῳ δικαιοῦσθε, τῆς χάριτος ἐξεπέσατε.
records.gloss: You were severed from Christ, you who in law are being justified; from the grace you fell away.
pieces: Any of you who look to the law to justify you have been cut off from {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}; you have fallen away from grace.

L.4: You were cut off from {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, you who are being justified in [the] law; you have fallen away from grace.

R.4: If you are trying to be put right with God by keeping the law, you have cut yourselves off from {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. You have left God's grace behind.

decisions.choice: justify: God declares a person to be in the right before him, acquitted and accepted
alternatives: to make a person morally good
decisions.reason: δικαιόω is a courtroom word. Galatians uses it for God's verdict that a person stands right with him (2:16-17, 3:8, 3:11, 3:24). Here Paul speaks of looking for that verdict "in law", by keeping it.

decisions.choice: "you who are trying to be justified": the present tense describes an attempt
alternatives: "you who are justified by the law", as a fact
decisions.reason: Paul has said that no one is justified by the law (2:16, 3:11), so the present δικαιοῦσθε describes what they are trying to do, not something achieved. οἵτινες ("you who", "whoever of you") points to any of them who take that path.

decisions.choice: cut off from Christ, with the bond to him made void
alternatives: "you have no more use for Christ"
decisions.reason: καταργέω with "from" means to be released or severed from something, so that it no longer has effect. Romans 7:2 and 7:6 use it of being released from the law. To seek justification by the law is to break the tie with Christ that faith made.

decisions.choice: fallen away from grace: lost hold of the gift by which God accepts them
alternatives: "fallen from grace" as moral failure or loss of reputation
decisions.reason: ἐκπίπτω means to fall out of or lose one's place. Grace here is God's free gift of acceptance (1:6, 2:21); someone who relies on the law has stepped out of the place where grace is received. Paul is not speaking of an ordinary sin.

decisions.choice: put right with God
decisions.reason: Readable says what the courtroom word means in plain words; Literal and Balanced keep "justified".

records.source: ἡμεῖς γὰρ πνεύματι ἐκ πίστεως ἐλπίδα δικαιοσύνης ἀπεκδεχόμεθα.
records.gloss: We for by [the] Spirit from faith [the] hope of righteousness eagerly await.
pieces: But we, by the Spirit and on the ground of faith, are eagerly waiting for the righteousness we hope for.

L.5: For we, by [the] Spirit, from faith, eagerly await [the] hope of righteousness.

R.5: But we, by the Spirit and through faith, wait eagerly for what we hope for: to hear God declare us righteous.

decisions.choice: by the Spirit: God's Spirit, given when they believed
decisions.reason: πνεύματι without the article still means God's Spirit, as in 3:3, 3:5 and 4:6: the Galatians received the Spirit by believing, not by doing what the law commands.

decisions.choice: the hope of righteousness: the righteousness hoped for, God's final verdict at the last day
alternatives: the hope that comes from being righteous now
decisions.reason: ἐλπίδα δικαιοσύνης most likely names what is hoped for: God's verdict of righteous, already given to faith (2:16) and still to be pronounced at the end. Paul could also mean the hope that belongs to those already made righteous. The two readings overlap: the Spirit and faith, not the law, carry believers to that day.

decisions.choice: "we" is emphatic, setting believers against those relying on the law
decisions.reason: ἡμεῖς stands first and is not needed for the verb. Paul sets "we" who wait by faith against "you who are trying to be justified in law" (verse 4).

decisions.choice: to hear God declare us righteous
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the reading chosen in m2; Literal and Balanced keep the phrase.

records.source: ἐν γὰρ Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ οὔτε περιτομή τι ἰσχύει οὔτε ἀκροβυστία, ἀλλὰ πίστις δι’ ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένη.
records.gloss: In for Christ Jesus neither circumcision anything is strong nor uncircumcision, but faith through love working.
pieces: For in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus, being circumcised or uncircumcised counts for nothing. What counts is faith at work through love.

L.6: For in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus neither circumcision has any force nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love.

R.6: When we belong to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus, it does not matter at all whether we are circumcised or not. What matters is faith that shows itself in love.

decisions.choice: faith working through love: faith shows its power in love
decisions.reason: ἐνεργουμένη is middle in sense here, as ἐνεργέω usually is in Paul: faith is active, and love is the way it works. The other reading, that love brings faith to life, puts the stress where Paul does not; faith is what justifies (2:16) and love is what it produces (5:13-14).

decisions.choice: circumcision and uncircumcision: being a Jew or a Gentile
decisions.reason: ἀκροβυστία literally means "foreskin", and Paul uses the pair for the two groups (2:7). In Christ neither condition gives a person any standing; 6:15 says the same.

decisions.choice: what counts is
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply the verb from the first clause ("has any power") so that the contrast reads clearly.

records.source: Ἐτρέχετε καλῶς· τίς ὑμᾶς ἐνέκοψεν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ μὴ πείθεσθαι;
records.gloss: You were running well; who you cut in on to the truth not to obey?
pieces: You had been running a good race. Who got in your way and turned you from obeying the truth?

L.7: You were running well; who cut in on you so that you do not obey the truth?

R.7: You were doing so well, like runners in a race. Who blocked your way and stopped you from following the truth?

decisions.choice: a race: someone cut in on the runners and blocked their way
alternatives: a general word for hindering, with no picture
decisions.reason: Ἐτρέχετε pictures the Christian life as a race, as Paul does in 2:2. ἐγκόπτω was used of breaking up a road or cutting in on a runner. The imperfect tense says they were running well up to that point.

decisions.choice: to obey the truth: to keep following the gospel they believed
alternatives: to be persuaded of the truth
decisions.reason: πείθω can mean both "be persuaded" and "obey". "The truth" is the truth of the gospel (2:5, 2:14). Verse 8 plays on the same root: the new "persuasion" is not from God.

decisions.choice: you had been running a good race
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the race so the picture is clear.

records.heading: Who blocked your way?

records.source: ἡ πεισμονὴ οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ καλοῦντος ὑμᾶς.
records.gloss: The persuasion [is] not from the [one] calling you.
pieces: That persuasion did not come from the one who calls you.

L.8: This persuasion [is] not from the one calling you.

R.8: That pressure to change did not come from God, who called you.

decisions.choice: persuasion: the pressure the agitators were putting on them
alternatives: the Galatians' own state of being persuaded
decisions.reason: πεισμονὴ is rare and could mean the act of persuading or the state of being persuaded. It follows the verb πείθω in verse 7 as a play on words: whatever has persuaded them now did not come from God.

decisions.choice: the one calling you is God
decisions.reason: Paul has already said that God called them by grace (1:6, 1:15). The present tense speaks of God as the one who calls.

decisions.choice: God
decisions.reason: Readable names God, as m2 explains.

records.source: μικρὰ ζύμη ὅλον τὸ φύραμα ζυμοῖ.
records.gloss: A little leaven whole the lump leavens.
pieces: A little yeast spreads through all the dough.

L.9: A little leaven leavens all of the lump.

R.9: It only takes a tiny bit of yeast to spread through a whole lump of dough.

decisions.choice: a proverb: a small thing spreads through the whole
decisions.reason: Paul uses the same saying in 1 Corinthians 5:6. ζύμη is leaven, a lump of old fermented dough mixed into new dough; a little works through the whole batch. Here it warns that the agitators, though few, and their teaching, though it seems a small step, will affect the whole church.

decisions.choice: yeast; spreads through
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the everyday word; Literal keeps "leaven" and the repeated root.

records.source: ἐγὼ πέποιθα εἰς ὑμᾶς ἐν κυρίῳ ὅτι οὐδὲν ἄλλο φρονήσετε· ὁ δὲ ταράσσων ὑμᾶς βαστάσει τὸ κρίμα, ὅστις ἐὰν ᾖ.
records.gloss: I am confident toward you in [the] Lord that nothing other you will think; the but [one] troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever if he may be.
pieces: In the Lord I am confident that you will not think otherwise. But the one who is unsettling you will bear God's judgment, whoever that may be.

L.10: I am confident about you in [the] Lord that you will think nothing other; but the one troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.

R.10: Because of the Lord, I trust that you will agree with me. But the person who is troubling you will face God's judgment, no matter who that is.

decisions.choice: Paul's confidence rests on the Lord, not on the Galatians
decisions.reason: "In the Lord" says where Paul's confidence comes from. The perfect πέποιθα speaks of a settled conviction.

decisions.choice: the one troubling you: whoever among the agitators, without exception
alternatives: a single leader of the agitators
decisions.reason: Elsewhere Paul speaks of several troublemakers (1:7, 5:12). The singular with "whoever he may be" most likely means any one of them, however important. It may point to one leader, but the letter does not name him.

decisions.choice: bear the judgment: God's judgment
decisions.reason: κρίμα with the article is the verdict that falls on such a person. As in 1:8-9, Paul leaves that judgment to God.

decisions.choice: God's judgment
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the judge (m3).

decisions.choice: you will agree with me
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what "nothing other" means: no view other than the gospel Paul taught them.

records.source: ἐγὼ δέ, ἀδελφοί, εἰ περιτομὴν ἔτι κηρύσσω, τί ἔτι διώκομαι;
records.gloss: I but, brothers, if circumcision still I preach, why still am I persecuted?
pieces: As for me, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, if I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted?

L.11: But I, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, if I still preach circumcision, why am I still persecuted?

R.11: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, if I were still telling people that they must be circumcised, why would people still be attacking me?

decisions.choice: "if I still preach circumcision": answering a claim that Paul himself required it
alternatives: Paul refers only to the time before he followed Christ
decisions.reason: The double ἔτι ("still ... still") suggests that someone was saying Paul preached circumcision when it suited him, perhaps pointing to Timothy (Acts 16:3) or to his life before his calling (1:13-14). What exactly lay behind the claim is not certain; Paul's answer is that his being persecuted proves it false.

decisions.choice: persecuted: opposed and attacked, by Jews and by those who wanted circumcision
decisions.reason: Paul's persecution came from those who saw his law-free gospel for Gentiles as a threat (4:29, 6:12; Acts 14:19).

records.source: ἄρα κατήργηται τὸ σκάνδαλον τοῦ σταυροῦ.
records.gloss: Then has been abolished the stumbling block of the cross.
pieces: In that case the cross would have stopped being a stumbling block.

L.11: Then the stumbling block of the cross has been abolished.

R.11: If I did, the message about the cross would no longer offend anyone.

decisions.choice: the stumbling block of the cross: what offends people about a crucified Messiah
decisions.reason: σκάνδαλον is a trap or something that makes people stumble. A Messiah who died on a cross offended Jews (1 Corinthians 1:23), and a message that the cross alone saves, without circumcision, offended those who wanted to keep the law's marks (6:12).

decisions.choice: an ironic conclusion: then the offense would be gone
alternatives: a real statement that the offense has been removed
decisions.reason: ἄρα draws the conclusion of the claim in the first sentence. If Paul preached circumcision, the cross would no longer offend anyone; but it does, as his persecution shows.

decisions.choice: in that case ... would
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make the irony plain by tying the sentence to the "if" of the one before.

records.source: ὄφελον καὶ ἀποκόψονται οἱ ἀναστατοῦντες ὑμᾶς.
records.gloss: Would that even will cut themselves off those unsettling you.
pieces: As for those who are stirring you up, I wish they would go the whole way and castrate themselves!

L.12: I wish that those unsettling you would even cut themselves off!

R.12: I wish the people who are upsetting you would go further than circumcision and castrate themselves!

decisions.choice: castrate themselves: a coarse play on circumcision
alternatives: cut themselves off from the church
decisions.reason: ἀποκόπτω means "cut off". Used of the body, and with "even" after a passage about circumcision, it most naturally means to cut off the male organ altogether. Paul says that if the agitators are so keen on cutting, they might go all the way. Some have read it as a wish that they would cut themselves off from the church, but that does not explain "even". The pagan priests of the goddess Cybele, known in Galatia, castrated themselves; Paul's words would put circumcision demanded as a condition on the same level.

decisions.choice: a wish that is not expected to come true
decisions.reason: ὄφελον with a future verb expresses a wish, here a bitter and sarcastic one.

decisions.choice: those unsettling you: stirring them up and turning them upside down
decisions.reason: ἀναστατόω is used of stirring up a revolt (Acts 17:6, 21:38); it is stronger than "troubling" in verse 10.

decisions.choice: castrate themselves
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say plainly what the verb means here (m1); Literal keeps "cut themselves off", with its double sense.

records.source: Ὑμεῖς γὰρ ἐπ’ ἐλευθερίᾳ ἐκλήθητε, ἀδελφοί· μόνον μὴ τὴν ἐλευθερίαν εἰς ἀφορμὴν τῇ σαρκί, ἀλλὰ διὰ τῆς ἀγάπης δουλεύετε ἀλλήλοις·
records.gloss: You for to freedom were called, brothers; only not the freedom into an opening for the flesh, but through the love serve as slaves one another;
pieces: You were called to be free, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}. Only do not let your freedom become an opening for the flesh. Instead, through love, be slaves to one another.

L.13: For you were called to freedom, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}; only [do] not [turn] the freedom into an opening for the flesh, but through love serve one another as slaves.

R.13: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, God called you to be free. But do not treat your freedom as a chance to give your sinful self what it wants. Instead, love one another and serve one another like slaves.

decisions.choice: the sinful human self opposed to the Spirit
decisions.reason: In 5:13-24 σαρκί is not the body as such but human life apart from God and turned against him: it has desires (5:16-17), works (5:19) and can be crucified (5:24), and it stands against the Spirit. The word keeps its link with the circumcised "flesh" the agitators boast in (6:12-13).

decisions.choice: an opening: a base from which to launch an attack
decisions.reason: ἀφορμὴν was used of a starting point or base for military operations. Freedom must not give the flesh a foothold.

decisions.choice: serve as slaves: freedom used to become one another's slaves in love
decisions.reason: δουλεύω is the verb of being a slave, the same root as the "slavery" of 5:1 and 4:3, 4:8-9. The paradox is deliberate: those freed from the law's yoke give themselves to one another out of love.

decisions.choice: your sinful self
decisions.reason: Readable says what "flesh" means here (m1); Literal and Balanced keep "flesh".

decisions.choice: God called you
decisions.reason: Readable names the one who called, as in 1:6 and 5:8.

decisions.choice: serve as slaves / be slaves / serve like slaves
decisions.reason: "Slave" at every level, as the style guide keeps it where slavery is set against freedom in the same sentence: those called to freedom become one another's slaves in love, a deliberate paradox (m3).

records.heading: Free to serve one another in love

records.source: ὁ γὰρ πᾶς νόμος ἐν ἑνὶ λόγῳ πεπλήρωται, ἐν τῷ· Ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου ὡς σεαυτόν.
records.gloss: The for whole law in one word has been fulfilled, in the: You shall love the neighbor of you as yourself.
pieces: The whole law comes to its fullness in one sentence: "You must love your neighbor as you love yourself."

L.14: For the whole law has been fulfilled in one word, in this: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself."

R.14: Everything the law asks is done when you keep this one command: "Love your neighbor as much as you love yourself."

decisions.choice: a quotation of Leviticus 19:18
decisions.reason: Paul quotes the command to love one's neighbor from Leviticus 19:18, in the words of the Greek translation of the Old Testament. Jesus named it as the second great command (Mark 12:31), and Paul uses it the same way in Romans 13:8-10.

decisions.choice: fulfilled: the law's whole aim is reached and done in love
alternatives: summed up only, as a summary
decisions.reason: πεπλήρωται is perfect: the law has been fulfilled. Paul does not only mean that one command sums up the rest; when people love, what the law was aiming at actually happens. Those who are not under the law (5:18) still fulfill it by love.

decisions.choice: one word: one saying, a single command
decisions.reason: λόγῳ here is one sentence of Scripture, not one word.

records.source: εἰ δὲ ἀλλήλους δάκνετε καὶ κατεσθίετε, βλέπετε μὴ ὑπ’ ἀλλήλων ἀναλωθῆτε.
records.gloss: If but one another you bite and devour, watch lest by one another you be consumed.
pieces: But if you keep biting one another and tearing each other apart, be careful, or you will end up destroying one another.

L.15: But if you bite and devour one another, watch lest you be used up by one another.

R.15: But if you keep attacking each other like wild animals, watch out! You will end up wiping each other out.

decisions.choice: biting, devouring, consuming: wild animals fighting until they destroy each other
decisions.reason: The three verbs picture animals tearing at one another; ἀναλίσκω means to use up or destroy entirely. The present tenses suggest the quarrels had already begun.

decisions.choice: attacking each other like wild animals
decisions.reason: Readable names the picture so it is not taken literally.

records.source: Λέγω δέ, πνεύματι περιπατεῖτε καὶ ἐπιθυμίαν σαρκὸς οὐ μὴ τελέσητε.
records.gloss: I say but, by [the] Spirit walk and [the] desire of flesh not not you will carry out.
pieces: This is what I mean: walk by the Spirit, and you will never carry out what the flesh desires.

L.16: But I say, walk by [the] Spirit, and you will certainly not carry out [the] desire of [the] flesh.

R.16: So this is what I am saying: let the Spirit guide your steps each day. Then you will never do what your sinful self wants.

decisions.choice: the sinful human self opposed to the Spirit
decisions.reason: In 5:13-24 σαρκὸς is not the body as such but human life apart from God and turned against him: it has desires (5:16-17), works (5:19) and can be crucified (5:24), and it stands against the Spirit. The word keeps its link with the circumcised "flesh" the agitators boast in (6:12-13).

decisions.choice: a promise: you will certainly not carry out what the flesh desires
alternatives: a second command: and do not carry out the flesh's desire
decisions.reason: οὐ μὴ with the aorist subjunctive is the strongest way Greek says "will not". It promises the result of walking by the Spirit; it is not a further command.

decisions.choice: walk by the Spirit: live day by day as the Spirit directs and empowers
decisions.reason: περιπατέω ("walk") is the usual biblical word for how a person lives. The dative πνεύματι says the Spirit is the power and guide of that life.

decisions.choice: let the Spirit guide your steps each day
decisions.reason: Readable explains the walking picture.

decisions.choice: your sinful self
decisions.reason: Readable says what "flesh" means here (m1).

records.heading: Walk by the Spirit

records.source: ἡ γὰρ σὰρξ ἐπιθυμεῖ κατὰ τοῦ πνεύματος, τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα κατὰ τῆς σαρκός, ταῦτα γὰρ ἀλλήλοις ἀντίκειται, ἵνα μὴ ἃ ἐὰν θέλητε ταῦτα ποιῆτε.
records.gloss: The for flesh desires against the Spirit, the and Spirit against the flesh, these for to one another are opposed, so that not whatever things you may want these you may do.
pieces: For the flesh sets its desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh. They are at war with each other, so that you are not free to do whatever you please.

L.17: For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh, for these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do whatever things you want.

R.17: What your sinful self wants is against what the Spirit wants, and what the Spirit wants is against your sinful self. The two are at war with each other. So you cannot just do whatever you feel like doing.

decisions.choice: the sinful human self opposed to the Spirit
decisions.reason: In 5:13-24 σὰρξ is not the body as such but human life apart from God and turned against him: it has desires (5:16-17), works (5:19) and can be crucified (5:24), and it stands against the Spirit. The word keeps its link with the circumcised "flesh" the agitators boast in (6:12-13).

decisions.choice: so that you do not simply do whatever you want: the conflict leaves no room for doing as you please
alternatives: the flesh keeps you from doing the good you want
the Spirit keeps you from doing what the flesh wants
decisions.reason: ἵνα can express purpose or result, and Paul does not say which wishes are blocked. The flesh may hinder the good a person wants (compare Romans 7:15-20), or the Spirit may hold back the flesh's desires, as verse 16 promises. Read with verse 13, the point seems to be that freedom is not doing as one likes: a person is in a battle and must follow the Spirit (verse 18).

decisions.choice: at war with each other
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable bring out the strength of the word for opposing.

decisions.choice: your sinful self
decisions.reason: Readable says what "flesh" means here (m1).

records.source: εἰ δὲ πνεύματι ἄγεσθε, οὐκ ἐστὲ ὑπὸ νόμον.
records.gloss: If but by [the] Spirit you are led, not you are under law.
pieces: But if the Spirit is leading you, you are not under the law.

L.18: But if you are led by [the] Spirit, you are not under [the] law.

R.18: But if the Spirit is leading you, then the law is not your master.

decisions.choice: under law: living under the law's rule as guardian and master
decisions.reason: Paul has used "under law" for the time before Christ, when the law held people as a guardian holds a child (3:23-25, 4:4-5). Those led by the Spirit are no longer under that regime, yet they are not left without guidance: the Spirit leads them.

decisions.choice: "if" describes what is true of believers: they are led by the Spirit
decisions.reason: εἰ with the present indicative assumes the condition; compare Romans 8:14, where all who are led by God's Spirit are God's children.

decisions.choice: the law is not your master
alternatives: you are not under the law
decisions.reason: Readable explains "under" as being ruled (m1).

records.source: φανερὰ δέ ἐστιν τὰ ἔργα τῆς σαρκός, ἅτινά ἐστιν πορνεία, ἀκαθαρσία, ἀσέλγεια, εἰδωλολατρία, φαρμακεία, ἔχθραι, ἔρις, ζῆλος, θυμοί, ἐριθεῖαι, διχοστασίαι, αἱρέσεις, φθόνοι, μέθαι, κῶμοι, καὶ τὰ ὅμοια τούτοις, ἃ προλέγω ὑμῖν καθὼς προεῖπον ὅτι οἱ τὰ τοιαῦτα πράσσοντες βασιλείαν θεοῦ οὐ κληρονομήσουσιν.
records.gloss: Evident and are the works of the flesh, which are sexual immorality, impurity, indecency, \v 20 idolatry, sorcery, hostilities, strife, jealousy, angers, rivalries, dissensions, factions, \v 21 envyings, drunkennesses, revelries, and the things like these, which I tell beforehand to you just as I said before, that the [ones] the such things practicing [the] kingdom of God not will inherit.
pieces: The works of the flesh are plain to see: sexual immorality, impurity, indecency,
idolatry, sorcery, hostility, quarreling, jealousy, fits of rage, selfish rivalry, divisions, factions,
envy, drunken bouts, wild partying, and other things like these. I am telling you now, as I told you before: people who live this way will not inherit the kingdom of God.

L.19: Now the works of the flesh are evident, which are sexual immorality, impurity, indecency,
L.20: idolatry, sorcery, hostilities, strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, selfish rivalries, dissensions, factions,
L.21: envyings, drunken bouts, revelries, and the things like these, about which I tell you beforehand, just as I said before, that those who practice such things will not inherit [the] kingdom of God.

R.19: It is easy to see what the sinful self does: sexual sin, impure living, shameless behavior,
R.20: worshiping idols, using magic, hating people, fighting, being jealous, losing your temper, putting yourself first, splitting into sides and groups,
R.21: envying others, getting drunk, wild parties, and other things like these. I warned you before, and I am warning you again: people who keep doing such things will not receive God's kingdom as their inheritance.

decisions.choice: the sinful human self opposed to the Spirit
decisions.reason: In 5:13-24 σαρκός is not the body as such but human life apart from God and turned against him: it has desires (5:16-17), works (5:19) and can be crucified (5:24), and it stands against the Spirit. The word keeps its link with the circumcised "flesh" the agitators boast in (6:12-13).

decisions.choice: sorcery: magic and spells, which often used drugs and potions
alternatives: the use of drugs or poisons in general
decisions.reason: φαρμακεία comes from the word for a drug, but in lists like this it means magic arts, in which potions were used to curse, charm or harm (compare Revelation 9:21, 18:23). It stands next to idolatry as a sin against God.

decisions.choice: selfish rivalry; factions: people splitting into parties
alternatives: "heresies" in the later sense of false doctrine
decisions.reason: ἐριθεῖαι is the self-seeking of someone out for himself or his party. αἱρέσεις here means groups that take sides against each other, as in 1 Corinthians 11:19, not yet a technical word for false teaching.

decisions.choice: those who practice such things: a settled way of life
alternatives: anyone who has ever done one of them
decisions.reason: The present participle πράσσοντες describes people who go on doing these things. Paul warns that such a life shows a person does not belong to God's kingdom; the same warning comes in 1 Corinthians 6:9-11, which speaks of people who were washed from such a life.

decisions.choice: Paul had warned them of this before, while he was with them
decisions.reason: προεῖπον ("I said before") points back to his teaching when he founded the churches (compare 1:9, 4:13).

decisions.choice: indecency / shameless behavior
decisions.reason: ἀσέλγεια is open, shameless indecency; Balanced and Readable use words a reader will understand without a dictionary.

decisions.choice: your sinful self
decisions.reason: Readable says what "flesh" means here (m1).

decisions.choice: receive God's kingdom as their inheritance
decisions.reason: Readable explains "inherit": to receive what belongs to God's children (4:7).

records.source: Ὁ δὲ καρπὸς τοῦ πνεύματός ἐστιν ἀγάπη, χαρά, εἰρήνη, μακροθυμία, χρηστότης, ἀγαθωσύνη, πίστις, πραΰτης, ἐγκράτεια· κατὰ τῶν τοιούτων οὐκ ἔστιν νόμος.
records.gloss: The but fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, long-suffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, \v 23 gentleness, self-control; against the such things not there is law.
pieces: But the fruit the Spirit produces is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness,
gentleness and self-control. No law stands against things like these.

L.22: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness,
L.23: gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law.

R.22: But the Spirit grows a different crop in us: love, joy and peace; patience with others, kindness and goodness; faithfulness,
R.23: gentleness and self-control. There is no law against things like these.

decisions.choice: the fruit of the Spirit: one harvest, which the Spirit produces
alternatives: separate fruits, any one of which a person may have
decisions.reason: καρπὸς is singular, set against the plural "works" of the flesh (verse 19). The qualities belong together as one crop that grows from the Spirit's life in a person, not as achievements of human effort.

decisions.choice: faithfulness: being reliable and true to others
decisions.reason: In this list of qualities shown toward others, πίστις means faithfulness, the sense it has in Romans 3:3 and Titus 2:10. Elsewhere in Galatians the same word means trust in Christ, but here it stands between goodness and gentleness as part of a person's character.

decisions.choice: peace: wholeness and harmony, with God and with one another
decisions.reason: εἰρήνη here stands against the strife and divisions of verse 20; it is peace among people as well as peace with God.

decisions.choice: patience: bearing with people for a long time without anger
decisions.reason: μακροθυμία is "long temper", slowness to anger, usually toward people who wrong or provoke us.

decisions.choice: against such things: the qualities just listed
decisions.reason: τοιούτων could be neuter ("such things") or masculine ("such people"). The meaning is close either way: no law forbids or condemns a life like this.

decisions.choice: faithfulness
decisions.reason: The key term is rendered "faithfulness" here because of its sense in this list (m2).

decisions.choice: the Spirit grows a different crop in us
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the picture of the fruit and the contrast with verse 19.

records.source: οἱ δὲ τοῦ Χριστοῦ τὴν σάρκα ἐσταύρωσαν σὺν τοῖς παθήμασιν καὶ ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις.
records.gloss: Those and of the Christ the flesh crucified with the passions and the desires.
pieces: Those who belong to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} have nailed the flesh to the cross, together with its passions and desires.

L.24: And those of the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} have crucified the flesh with the passions and the desires.

R.24: People who belong to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} have put their sinful self to death on the cross, with all its strong feelings and desires.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "those of Christ"
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts add "Jesus" after "Christ". The SBLGNT text follows early manuscripts that have "Christ" alone. The meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: the sinful human self opposed to the Spirit
decisions.reason: In 5:13-24 σάρκα is not the body as such but human life apart from God and turned against him: it has desires (5:16-17), works (5:19) and can be crucified (5:24), and it stands against the Spirit. The word keeps its link with the circumcised "flesh" the agitators boast in (6:12-13).

decisions.choice: they crucified the flesh: a decisive act when they came to belong to Christ
alternatives: a continuing effort to kill the flesh
decisions.reason: ἐσταύρωσαν is an aorist active verb: it looks back to something done. In 2:19-20 Paul has been crucified with Christ, and in 6:14 the world has been crucified to him. Those who belong to Christ have taken his side against the flesh once for all; walking by the Spirit (verse 25) lives that out.

decisions.choice: nailed the flesh to the cross
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the picture of crucifixion vivid; Literal keeps "crucified".

decisions.choice: put their sinful self to death on the cross
decisions.reason: Readable says what "flesh" means here (m2) and what crucifying it does.

records.source: εἰ ζῶμεν πνεύματι, πνεύματι καὶ στοιχῶμεν.
records.gloss: If we live by [the] Spirit, by [the] Spirit also let us keep in line.
pieces: Since our life comes from the Spirit, let us also follow the Spirit's lead in each step we take.

L.25: If we live by [the] Spirit, let us also keep in line with [the] Spirit.

R.25: The Spirit has given us life. So let us also follow the Spirit, one step at a time.

decisions.choice: "if we live by the Spirit": since we do
decisions.reason: εἰ with the indicative assumes the fact: believers have life from the Spirit (3:3, 3:5, 4:6).

decisions.choice: keep in line with the Spirit: follow the Spirit's lead step by step
decisions.reason: στοιχέω means to stand or move in a line, as soldiers in rank or plants in a row, and so to follow a rule or pattern. Paul uses the same verb in 6:16. It is a different word from "walk" in verse 16.

decisions.choice: follow the Spirit's lead
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable express the picture of keeping in line in plain words.

records.source: μὴ γινώμεθα κενόδοξοι, ἀλλήλους προκαλούμενοι, ἀλλήλοις φθονοῦντες.
records.gloss: Not let us become vainglorious, one another challenging, one another envying.
pieces: We must not become people hungry for empty praise, who challenge one another and envy one another.

L.26: Let us not become vainglorious, challenging one another, envying one another.

R.26: We should not show off to get people's praise. We should not try to beat each other or be jealous of each other.

decisions.choice: vainglorious: hungry for empty praise
decisions.reason: κενόδοξοι is made from "empty" and "glory": someone eager for honor that has no worth.

decisions.choice: two sides of the same sin: those who feel above others challenge them; those who feel below envy them
decisions.reason: προκαλέομαι is to call someone out, to challenge him to a contest. φθονέω is to envy. Both come from wanting empty glory, and both destroy the love Paul has called for (verses 13-15).

decisions.choice: vainglorious
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the two parts of the Greek word.
